KUBERNETES ROLLOUT SAFETY CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Will your Kubernetes rollout drop live requests?

RollingUpdate promises that Kubernetes replaces pods gradually. It does not promise that a pod is ready before traffic reaches it, or that it has stopped receiving traffic before it shuts down. Those two gaps are why a deploy that reports success can still serve a burst of connection errors — and nothing in kubectl rollout status will ever mention it. Paste your Deployment YAML below.

Nothing is uploaded. The manifest you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device; this tool makes no network calls of its own and never touches your cluster.

1. Paste your manifests

A Deployment, and ideally the PodDisruptionBudget and Service that select it. Multiple documents separated by --- are fine, and a kind: List wrapper is unwrapped — so the whole output of kubectl get deploy,pdb,svc -o yaml works, as does a rendered Helm or Kustomize template. Including the Service is worth it: without one, nothing in the manifest says which container answers a request, so every container is checked and a sidecar will show up alongside your application.

Paste a Deployment above and click Check.

Findings

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same engine, zero dependencies, no cluster access:

node check.mjs                     # scan every .yaml under the current directory
node check.mjs k8s/production      # scan one directory or one file
node check.mjs --format json       # machine-readable
node check.mjs --list-checks       # exactly what is checked, and at what severity
node check.mjs --fail-on-risk      # exit 2 if a rollout can drop requests

Save the three files this page itself runs on — check.mjs, engine.mjs and yaml.mjs — into one directory. Node's standard library only, nothing to install, no network calls, no kubeconfig. Render your Helm chart or Kustomize overlay first (helm template / kubectl kustomize) and pipe the output to a file, then wire --fail-on-risk into CI so a newly-added Deployment without a readinessProbe is caught before it merges.

What it checks

The whole list — there is nothing hidden behind it.

    Common questions

    My rollout says zero downtime. Why would it drop requests?

    Because "RollingUpdate" only promises that Kubernetes replaces pods gradually. It does not promise that a pod is ready before it receives traffic, or that it has stopped receiving traffic before it shuts down. Without a readinessProbe, a pod joins the load balancer the instant its process starts — every request arriving before the app has booted gets an error. Without a preStop delay, the container can exit before the pod's removal has propagated to every kube-proxy and ingress controller, so proxies keep sending it connections that are then refused. Both are invisible in a rollout that reports success.

    Why does a missing preStop hook matter if my app handles SIGTERM?

    Because handling SIGTERM correctly is not the problem. When a pod is deleted, two things start at the same moment and neither waits for the other: the kubelet sends SIGTERM, and the endpoints controller begins removing the pod from EndpointSlice. That removal has to reach every kube-proxy and every ingress controller before they stop routing to it, and that propagation is not instant. A perfectly behaved app that shuts down promptly on SIGTERM can therefore be gone while proxies are still sending it new connections. A preStop hook that does nothing but wait gives the removal time to land before shutdown begins.

    Does a clean result mean my deploy is zero-downtime?

    No. This checks a specific, named list of manifest-level configurations — you can see the whole list with --list-checks, and there is nothing hidden behind it. It cannot know how long your application takes to drain a connection, whether your readinessProbe actually tests the dependencies a real request needs, whether your ingress controller honours EndpointSlice updates promptly, or whether a database migration in the same release is backwards compatible. A clean result means these checks found nothing; it is not a guarantee about your deploy.

    Does this tool connect to my cluster?

    No, and it has no way to. It reads YAML text and nothing else — no kubeconfig, no credentials, no API server, no network calls at all. The browser page parses what you paste on your own device, and the CLI reads files from your own disk. That is what makes it safe to run against production manifests in CI without granting it any cluster access, because there is none to grant.

    What about StatefulSets, DaemonSets and Argo Rollouts?

    Only Deployment and PodDisruptionBudget are judged, and a Service is read (not judged) to work out which container receives traffic. Other kinds are listed as skipped rather than silently ignored, so you can see what was not looked at. StatefulSet and DaemonSet rollouts have genuinely different ordering semantics, and reporting Deployment rules against them would produce confident wrong answers — which is worse than abstaining.

    Why is the default maxUnavailable of 25% not flagged?

    Because at most replica counts it is safe. Kubernetes rounds maxUnavailable down and maxSurge up, so at 3 replicas the 25%/25% default resolves to maxUnavailable 0 and maxSurge 1 — a new pod starts and becomes ready before any old pod is removed. Flagging that would make the tool cry wolf on the majority of real manifests. It is reported only when the resolved number actually reaches the replica count, which is when every pod really can be down at once.

    More: why your Kubernetes rollout drops requests. Already run kube-score? See how this checker compares on the rollout question specifically. This checks whether a rollout is safe, not whether the manifest's apiVersion itself will survive the next Kubernetes upgrade — a manifest can pass every check here and still fail to apply outright on a newer cluster. See Kubernetes Deprecated API Check for that, a separate failure class entirely.

    No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not a production-readiness audit, a security review, or a guarantee that your deploy is free of downtime, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, including testing any suggested change against your own workload before applying it to production. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

    Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, save check.mjs, engine.mjs and yaml.mjs and run them yourself.

    Everything runs in your browser. The manifest you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors, and the tool makes no network calls. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

    A safe rollout is only one part of a delivery pipeline that does not break: Pinned Actions Check asks whether the workflow that builds and ships this image is pinned to immutable references, Docker Base Image Pin Check asks the same of the FROM lines in the image itself, and SQL Migration Lock Check asks whether the schema change riding along with this release locks the database while the new pods come up — four slices of the same "does shipping this change break something quietly?" question.

    Free and open source. If this caught a rollout that would have dropped requests, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-kube-score.html.text:
kube-score vs a rollout safety check

A comparison · back to the rollout safety checker

These tools are often mentioned in the same breath and answer different questions. This page says which is which, including where the other one is the better choice. It describes kube-score as a category of tool — a general manifest linter, alongside Polaris and kubeaudit — from its published behaviour; it is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or a benchmark against any of them.

The short version

Should I use kube-score or this checker?

Both, for different jobs. kube-score is a broad manifest linter: it scores a manifest across dozens of rules spanning resource limits, security contexts, image tags, network policies and probes, and it is the better choice when you want one gate covering general manifest hygiene. This checker asks a single question — can this rolling update or node drain drop a live request? — and answers it with the causal chain rather than a rule name. Use the broad linter as your standing CI gate, and this one when you are specifically investigating errors that appear during deploys.

General manifest linterThis checker
Question askedDoes this manifest follow recommended practice across many dimensions?Can this rollout or node drain drop a live request?
OutputA score and a list of rule resultsFindings at two levels, each with the user-visible consequence and the YAML fix
ScopeMost workload kinds, many rule categoriesDeployment and PodDisruptionBudget only; other kinds listed as skipped
Relational checksGenerally per-fieldGrace period vs. preStop duration; maxUnavailable vs. replicas; PDB vs. replicas; liveness vs. readiness
InstallGo binary, container image, or Krew pluginNothing in the browser; two files on Node 18+ for the CLI
Cluster accessOptional, for some checksNone, ever — it reads YAML text and makes no network calls

Where they genuinely differ

Does this checker duplicate kube-score's probe rules?

They overlap on the readinessProbe rule and diverge everywhere else. The checks here that a general linter does not typically make are the relational ones: whether terminationGracePeriodSeconds is long enough to cover the preStop hook it is paired with, whether maxUnavailable resolves — after Kubernetes' round-down arithmetic — to the full replica count, whether the livenessProbe is a copy of the readinessProbe, and whether a PodDisruptionBudget is satisfiable at the Deployment's replica count. Each of those is a relationship between two fields, sometimes in two different resources, rather than a property of one field.

The grace-period case is the clearest example of why that distinction matters. A manifest with a 30-second preStop hook and the default 30-second grace period passes any per-field check: it has a preStop hook, and it has a grace period. The defect is only visible when the two are read together — SIGKILL lands at the moment preStop returns, so the application never drains at all, and the configuration is worse than having no preStop hook while looking considerably more careful.

Why does this tool not score my manifest?

Because a score answers "how am I doing?" and the question here is "will this specific thing break?". A score of 7/10 does not tell you whether the three missing points are the ones that drop requests. Findings are reported at two levels only — it can drop requests, or it is worth reviewing — and each one names the resource, the container, what a user experiences when it fires, and the YAML that fixes it.

Can I run this without installing anything?

Yes. The browser page needs no install at all and uploads nothing — paste the manifest and read the result. The CLI is two files of plain JavaScript that run on Node 18 or later with no dependencies, no Go toolchain, no container image and no kubeconfig. kube-score is distributed as a Go binary, container image and Krew plugin, which is a better fit if you already manage tooling that way.

When the other tool is the right answer

  • You want one CI gate covering manifest hygiene broadly — resource limits, security contexts, image tags, network policy. Use the general linter; this checker covers none of that.
  • You need StatefulSet, DaemonSet, CronJob or Job coverage. This tool analyzes Deployments only and says so rather than guessing.
  • You want a policy engine with custom rules you write yourself (Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper). This tool's checks are fixed and deliberately few.
  • You want a trend line across many services. A score is the right shape for that; a findings list is not.

Try it on one manifest. Paste a Deployment and see whether its rollout can drop requests. Nothing is uploaded, no cluster access is needed, and --list-checks shows the complete rule list before you trust any of it.

It describes other tools from their published behaviour and is not affiliated with or endorsed by any of them; it is not a benchmark, and their capabilities change over time — check their current documentation before choosing. Nothing here is a production-readiness audit or a guarantee about your deploy.

why-your-kubernetes-rollout-drops-reques.text:
Why your Kubernetes rollout drops requests

A practical guide · back to the rollout safety checker

A RollingUpdate deploy reports success. kubectl rollout status says the deployment is available. And a handful of users got a 502 or a connection reset while it was happening — not enough to page anyone, just enough to show up as a small, unexplained error spike that recurs on exactly the days you deploy.

This is not a bug in Kubernetes, and it is not usually a bug in the application either. It is the default behaviour of a manifest that has not been told otherwise. There are two separate races, one on each side of a pod's life, and they need different fixes.

Race one: traffic arrives before the pod can serve it

Why does a pod receive traffic before it is ready?

Because without a readinessProbe, Ready is defined as "the container process started". Kubernetes has no other way to know whether the application inside can serve a request, so it assumes it can. The Service adds the pod to its EndpointSlice immediately and the load balancer starts routing to it — while the app is still opening database connections, loading configuration, or warming a cache. Every request that lands in that window fails, on every rollout, and the rollout still reports success.

The fix is a readiness probe that actually fails while the app cannot serve:

readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /readyz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 2

The endpoint matters as much as the probe. A /readyz that returns 200 from a static handler proves only that the HTTP server is listening — which is almost the same thing as no probe at all. It should check the dependencies a real request needs, and report not-ready while any of them is unavailable.

Race two: traffic arrives after the pod has been told to stop

Why does a pod receive traffic after it has been told to shut down?

Because pod deletion starts two independent processes at the same instant, and neither waits for the other. The kubelet sends SIGTERM to the container. Separately, the endpoints controller removes the pod from EndpointSlice, and that removal then has to propagate to every kube-proxy on every node and to every ingress controller. Propagation takes time. An application that shuts down promptly and correctly on SIGTERM can therefore finish before the proxies have stopped routing to it, and every connection they open in that window is refused.

This one surprises people because the application is behaving well. Handling SIGTERM quickly makes it worse, not better: the faster the container exits, the wider the window in which proxies are still sending it work.

The fix is a preStop hook whose entire job is to wait, so the removal has time to land before shutdown begins:

lifecycle:
  preStop:
    sleep:
      seconds: 10          # Kubernetes 1.29+
      # older clusters:
      # exec:
      #   command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45

How long should the preStop sleep be?

Long enough for EndpointSlice removal to reach every proxy, which depends on cluster size and ingress controller. Five to fifteen seconds is a common starting point, and the way to tune it is to measure: send steady traffic, delete a pod, and see whether any request fails. The important part is that terminationGracePeriodSeconds must exceed the preStop wait plus the longest request the application needs to finish — the grace period covers both, and SIGKILL at the end of it does not care what is still in flight.

That last point is the trap worth stating plainly. The grace period clock starts when the pod is deleted, not when preStop returns. A 30-second preStop under the default 30-second grace period means the container is killed at the exact moment it was finally asked to shut down, so it never drains at all — a configuration that looks more careful than having no preStop hook, and behaves worse.

The rollout arithmetic

Kubernetes resolves maxUnavailable by rounding down and maxSurge by rounding up. The 25%/25% default at 3 replicas therefore means maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 — a replacement starts and becomes ready before anything is removed, which is the behaviour you want. It is worth knowing the default is usually fine, because the instinct on reading an article like this one is to change every setting, and most of the damage here comes from a value someone set deliberately:

strategy:
  rollingUpdate:
    maxUnavailable: 0     # never drop below the current capacity
    maxSurge: 1           # start one extra, wait for Ready, then retire one

Does a PodDisruptionBudget help during a rollout?

Not directly — a Deployment's own rollout is governed by maxUnavailable and maxSurge, not by the budget. A PodDisruptionBudget governs other voluntary disruptions, and the one that matters most is a node drain during a cluster upgrade, which is otherwise free to evict every replica of a workload at once. It is also possible to set a budget that can never be satisfied (minAvailable equal to the replica count), and that failure is unusually quiet: kubectl drain does not error, it blocks and retries indefinitely, so the upgrade appears to hang.

Check your own manifest. The rollout safety checker reads a Deployment and reports every one of these, with the YAML to fix each. It runs in your browser or as a zero-dependency CLI, never connects to a cluster, and uploads nothing.

A checklist, in the order they bite

  1. readinessProbe that fails while the app cannot serve — otherwise traffic arrives too early, every rollout.
  2. preStop wait so endpoint removal propagates before shutdown starts.
  3. terminationGracePeriodSeconds greater than the preStop wait plus your longest request.
  4. maxUnavailable: 0 with maxSurge: 1 when capacity is tight, so the service never dips below its current size.
  5. startupProbe for anything slow to boot, so the livenessProbe does not kill it mid-startup.
  6. A livenessProbe that is not a copy of the readinessProbe, so a slow dependency removes a pod from rotation instead of restarting it.
  7. A PodDisruptionBudget below the replica count, so a node drain can make progress but not take everything.
